_metadata.title: Crop Gene Editing Regulation Status by Country
_metadata.source: Heaton M, Ngure GM & Daujotaite, 2026, Crop Gene Editing Regulation Tracker

statuses.distinct: GE recognised as distinct from GM

_metadata.notes: Countries not listed have no data or unclassified status. The United Kingdom is subdivided by nation using ISO 3166-2 codes in the 'subdivisions' block.

032.name: Argentina
032.legislation: Ministry of Economy, Secretariat of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries. Resolution No. 24/2026
032.summary: Argentina was the first country in the world to establish a regulatory framework specifically for gene-edited crops, through Decision 173/2015. Gene-edited products without foreign DNA are classified as conventional and exempt from GMO regulation. This product-based, foreign-DNA criterion has become an international regulatory standard — the 'Argentina model'.
032.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Developers submit a dossier to CONABIA, which determines whether the product contains stable foreign DNA.

036.name: Australia
036.legislation: Australian government, department of health, office of the Gene Technology Regulator
036.regulatory_body: Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FANZ) and Gene Technology Regulator (GTR)
036.summary: SDN-1 organisms are exempt from being regulated as GMOs under the Gene Technology Act 2000. in 2025, FANZ updated the definitions of 'novel DNA' and 'novel food' to allow outcome-based evaluation, meaning transgene-free GEd crops no longer classify as GM food.

040.name: Austria
040.legislation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 of the European Parliament and of the Council on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products
040.regulatory_body: European Commission and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)
040.summary: EU Parliament has voted to adopt new rules granting use of gene edited plants that are climate and pest resistant to support food security. The new EU rules split regulation of EU cultivate or imported products into one of two "New Genomic Techniques" (NGT) groups: NGT-1 (conventional-like) and NGT-2 (GMO-like). The EU Commission has prepared an implementation strategy of Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products to ensure the EU NGT framework becomes fully functional on 17 July 2028.
040.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. National authorities must verify that NGT plants belong to category 1 (NGT-1), but their offspring do not need to be subsequently verified.

076.name: Brazil
076.legislation: Ministry of Science, Technology, Innovation, and Communications. Normative Resolution CTNBio No. 16/2018
076.summary: CTNBio established a framework for gene-edited crops through Normative Resolution No. 16 (RN16), issued 15 January 2018. RN16 defines 'Innovative Precision Improvement Techniques' (TIMPs) and allows developers to seek a determination on GMO classification. Products without recombinant DNA/RNA in the final product are eligible for non-GMO classification. In December 2024, MARA issued five biosafety certificates for gene-edited events, including the first gene-edited rice event approved for domestic cultivation.
076.approach: Product-based, consultation procedure. Products without recombinant DNA/RNA in the final product are classified as conventional.

854.name: Burkina Faso
854.legislation: Guide technique pour la réglementation de la biotechnologie moderne : Édition génomique
854.regulatory_body: National Biosafety Agency (Agence Nationale de Biosécurité, ANB)
854.summary: Burkina Faso established the National Biosafety Agency in 2005 and published genome editing guidance documents excluding gene-edited products devoid of foreign genetic material from GMO regulation. In July 2024, the ANB authorised the use of genome-edited rice lines to combat bacterial blight (Decision No. 2023-000122/MESRI/SG/ANB/DG), representing one of the earliest practical applications of genome editing in West Africa.
854.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Gene-edited products without foreign genetic material excluded from GMO regulation.

124.name: Canada
124.legislation: Health Canada, Guidance on Products of Plant Breeding (Novel Food Regulations, Division 28). CFIA Guidelines 2022
124.regulatory_body: Health Canada and Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA)
124.summary: Canada's regulatory system evaluates crops based on novelty of traits rather than breeding method. In May 2022, Health Canada published updated guidance clarifying that gene-edited crops meeting criteria for non-novel food are treated as conventional and do not require pre-market safety assessment. In May 2024, CFIA confirmed that gene-edited plants used in livestock feed are safe. A voluntary transparency initiative allows developers to notify Health Canada of non-novel gene-edited products.
124.approach: Product-based, trait-focused. Gene-edited crops without novel traits are treated as conventional and exempt from pre-market safety evaluation.

152.name: Chile
152.legislation: Ministry of Agriculture, SAG. Draft Resolution on NBTs (open for public consultation, January 2026)
152.summary: Chile has operated an informal case-by-case evaluation procedure since 2017 under Resolution No. 1523/2001. A draft resolution published for public consultation on 7 January 2026 would formalise this as a mandatory administrative process with a defined 20 working-day determination timeline. The draft explicitly excludes insertions of alleles from the same species from the definition of 'new combination of genetic material'. As of May 2026, the draft has not yet entered into force, pending publication in the Diario Oficial.
152.approach: Informal case-by-case procedure pending formalisation. Based on whether product contains a new combination of genetic material.

156.name: China
156.legislation: Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs (MARA). Guidelines for Safety Evaluation of Gene-Edited Plants for Agricultural Use (Trial), January 2022. Rules for Review of Gene-Edited Plants for Agricultural Use (Trial), April 2023
156.regulatory_body: Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs (MARA)
156.summary: MARA issued China's first gene-editing guidelines in January 2022, establishing application procedures for gene-edited plants without exogenous genes. These plants undergo a simplified safety evaluation compared to traditional GMOs, bypassing the lengthy multi-phase field trial process. In April 2023, MARA issued supplementary rules clarifying classification criteria. MARA has begun issuing biosafety certificates for gene-edited crop events. Plants that introduce exogenous genes remain subject to full GMO safety evaluation.
156.approach: Product-based, streamlined evaluation. Gene-edited plants without exogenous genes undergo simplified safety assessment compared to full GMO review.

170.name: Colombia
170.legislation: Colombian Institute of Agriculture and Livestock (ICA). Resolution No. 00022991/2022
170.summary: Colombia's framework was originally established by ICA Resolution No. 29299/2018 and extended by Resolution No. 00022991 (November 2022), which broadened scope to cover animals in addition to crop plants. Only products containing stable foreign genetic material are classified as Living Modified Organisms. Products without foreign DNA are treated as conventional.
170.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Central criterion is presence or absence of stable foreign genetic material.

188.name: Costa Rica
188.summary: Costa Rica updated its biotechnology regulatory framework in November 2023, facilitating the utilisation of innovative biotechnologies and reducing barriers to common applications of modern biotechnology. Under the new regulation, products created with innovative biotechnologies including gene editing are treated as equivalent to conventional products. A genome-edited banana variety resistant to sigatoka and fusarium wilt was expected to be the first genome-edited product commercialised in Costa Rica in 2024.
188.approach: Product-based. Gene-edited products treated as equivalent to conventional products.

218.name: Ecuador
218.legislation: Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock, and Fisheries. Ministerial Agreement No. 063/2023
218.regulatory_body: Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock, and Fisheries (MAGAP)
218.summary: Ecuador operates within a constrained framework — Article 401 of the 2008 Constitution declares Ecuador a GMO-free country. However, Ministerial Agreement No. 063/2023 established that only organisms containing recombinant or foreign DNA qualify as GMOs, creating a definitional exemption for transgene-free gene-edited products. The first application under this framework was submitted in October 2024 for a gene-edited banana variety developed in response to Fusarium wilt TR4 pressure.
218.approach: Definitional exclusion. Transgene-free gene-edited products fall outside the GMO definition under the Organic Code of the Environment (2019), without overriding the constitutional prohibition.

222.name: El Salvador
222.legislation: Inter-ministerial Technical Resolution RT 65:06.01:18 (2019), signed with Honduras and Guatemala
222.summary: El Salvador is a signatory to the 2019 inter-ministerial Technical Resolution (RT 65:06.01:18) with Honduras and Guatemala, agreeing that gene-edited crops without transgenic DNA should be regulated as conventional crops on a case-by-case basis. The agreement requires each country to create a national advisory committee for risk assessment of living modified organisms for agricultural use. Full domestic implementation of the streamlined procedures has been anticipated but not confirmed.
222.approach: Product-based (under regional agreement). Gene-edited products without transgenic DNA to be treated as conventional.

231.name: Ethiopia
231.legislation: Guideline for the Regulation of Genome Edited Plants in Ethiopia
231.summary: The guideline provide a triage instrument that determines whether a given edited plant falls under the existing Biosafety (Amendment) Proclamation No. 896/2015 or is exempted and handled as a conventional variety. Edits are non-regulated where they are deletions/knock-outs with no foreign genetic material remaining, insertions from sexually compatible species with same-species regulatory elements, or processed products containing no inserted foreign DNA. They are regulated where foreign genes from non-compatible species are inserted, where selectable/reporter markers persist in the end product. The 'Application for Early Consultation on Genome Editing Technology' is embedded at the back of the guideline (pages 4–6)

268.name: Georgia
268.summary: Georgia adopted a ban in 2017 on gene-edited plants for cultivation, import, and export.
268.approach: Prohibitive. Gene-edited plants banned from cultivation, import, and export. GE medical research is taking place in the country.

288.name: Ghana
288.legislation: Guidelines for Genome Editing Applications in Ghana
288.summary: Ghana's NBA published Guidelines on Genome Editing on 30 October 2023, providing procedural guidance on which genome-edited organisms fall under the Biosafety Act 2011 (Act 831). Ghana joined Nigeria, Kenya, and Malawi as the fourth African country with validated genome-editing guidelines. The guidelines provide clear processes for risk assessment, management, and decision-making through scientifically sound, case-by-case evaluations, distinguishing genome-edited products without foreign DNA from regulated GMOs.
288.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Risk assessment determines whether genome-edited products fall under the Biosafety Act.

320.name: Guatemala
320.legislation: Ministerio de Agricultura, Ganadería y Alimentación (MAGA). Resolution No. UA 60-2019. Inter-ministerial Technical Resolution RT 65:06.01:18
320.regulatory_body: Ministerio de Agricultura, Ganadería y Alimentación (MAGA)
320.summary: Guatemala adopted Resolution No. UA 60-2019, establishing a regulatory pathway for gene-edited crops. As part of the 2019 inter-ministerial Technical Resolution (RT 65:06.01:18) signed with Honduras and El Salvador, Guatemala exempts gene-edited organisms without stable integration of exogenous DNA from GMO regulation. Products are evaluated on a case-by-case basis, with determination of gene-edited plant classification falling under MAGA jurisdiction.
320.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Gene-edited products without exogenous DNA regulated as conventional.

340.name: Honduras
340.legislation: SENASA. Streamlined authorisation procedure for NBTs, 2019. Inter-ministerial Technical Resolution RT 65:06.01:18
340.regulatory_body: National Service of Agrifood Health and Safety (SENASA), National Biotechnology and Agricultural Biosafety Committee (CNBBA)
340.summary: Honduras became the first country in Central America to regulate products of new breeding techniques (NBTs) when SENASA published a resolution establishing a streamlined authorisation procedure in 2019. As part of the inter-ministerial Technical Resolution (RT 65:06.01:18) signed with Guatemala and El Salvador, gene-edited crops that do not fulfil the definition of transgenic GMOs are regulated as conventional crops. The simplified procedure shortens approval timelines for gene-edited products.
340.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Gene-edited products without transgenic DNA regulated as conventional crops under streamlined procedure.

356.name: India
356.legislation: Department of Biotechnology (DBT). Guidelines for Safety Assessment of Genome Edited Plants, 2022
356.summary: In May 2022, the Department of Biotechnology issued final guidelines exempting genome-edited plants without foreign DNA from the Rules 1989 framework implemented by the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC). Researchers using gene-editing technology to modify plant genomes without introducing foreign genes no longer require GEAC approval. The Institutional Biosafety Committee monitors genome-edited plants under containment until confirmed free from foreign DNA. The guidelines align India's framework with other major food-producing countries.
356.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Genome-edited plants free of foreign DNA are exempt from GEAC approval under Rules 1989.

360.name: Indonesia
360.legislation: BPOM Regulation No. 19/2024 on Supervision of Genetically Engineered Food. Government Regulation No. 21 of 2005 regarding Biosafety of Genetically Modified Products
360.regulatory_body: National Agency for Drug and Food Control (BPOM), GM Products Biosafety Commission
360.summary: Indonesia issued Regulation No. 19/2024 on the Supervision of Genetically Engineered Food on 18 November 2024, introducing food safety standards for genome editing. Food produced via genome editing is classified as either GM or non-GM based on assessment by the GM Products Biosafety Commission, in accordance with Government Regulation No. 21 of 2005. Mandatory labeling applies to packaged food containing at least 5% genetically engineered DNA, with a 12-month compliance grace period.
360.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Classification as GM or non-GM determined by the GM Products Biosafety Commission based on mechanism of genetic repair.

376.name: Israel
376.summary: Israel's NCTP announced in 2017 and clarified in 2019 that transgene-free plants are exempt from GEd regulation on a case-by-case basis. Applications to work with GE products must be approved by the NCTP, which also seeks input from the National Committee for Experiments (NCE). Under the regulation, certain product categories would be exempt from labelling requirements, including: 1. Products not containing foreign DNA or protein, 2. Products with less than 0.9% of the product being comprised of GE ingredients
376.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Gene-edited products without foreign genetic material excluded from GMO regulation.

392.name: Japan
392.legislation: Ministry of the Environment notification on genome-edited organisms under the Cartagena Act (February 2019). MAFF procedures for biodiversity information (October 2019). MHLW notification procedures for genome-edited foods (October 2019)
392.regulatory_body: Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF), Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)
392.summary: Japan established its genome-editing regulatory framework in 2019 through coordinated notifications across multiple ministries. The Ministry of the Environment ruled that SDN-1 organisms (without foreign DNA) are non-LMO under the Cartagena Act, while SDN-2 and SDN-3 remain regulated. MAFF issued procedures for biodiversity notification, and MHLW established food safety notification procedures. Gene-edited foods can be sold without safety evaluations provided they meet SDN-1 criteria, though developers must notify the government. Japan was among the first countries to commercialise gene-edited foods, with a GABA-enriched tomato reaching market in 2021.
392.approach: Notification-based. SDN-1 products (no foreign DNA) exempt from GMO regulation but require pre-market notification to relevant ministries.

404.name: Kenya
404.legislation: Guidelines for Determining the Regulatory Process of Genome Editing Techniques in Kenya (Revision No. 01, reference NBA/TEC/ML/11)
404.regulatory_body: National Biosafety Authority (NBA) and Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS)
404.summary: The NBA regulates all activities involving GMO under the 2009 Act. The genome-editing guideline creates a case by case mechanism to decide whether a given edited organism counts as a GMO (and so falls under the Act) or not. An applicant submits an Early Consultation Form (Annex 1) with a fee, and the NBA returns a decision within 30 working days. The decisive test is whether foreign genetic material remains in the final product. If it does, the product enters the full GMO risk-assessment and approval pathway. If the product is transgene free, it falls outside the Act and is handled as conventional by KEPHIS.

442.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. National authorities must verify that NGT plants belong to category 1 (NGT-1), but their offspring do not need to be subsequently verified.

450.name: Madagascar
450.summary: Madagascar has prohibited the cultivation of gene-edited plants. Institutional capacity in biosafety regulation remains limited, and strengthening the necessary structures and institutions is considered a prerequisite before genome editing experimentation can be considered.
450.approach: Prohibitive. Gene-edited plants banned from cultivation.

454.name: Malawi
454.regulatory_body: Ministry of Natural Resources and Climate Change (MNRCC) and National Biosafety Regulatory Committee (NBRC)
454.summary: Malawi approved its Genome Editing Guidelines in August 2022, becoming the third African country (after Nigeria and Kenya) to adopt such guidelines. The guidelines provide a step-by-step procedure for regulating genome editing and products, clarifying which products are exempt from GMO regulation. Products containing novel combinations of DNA are regulated as GMOs, while those without foreign DNA are treated as conventional. The guidelines were developed in consultation with biosafety stakeholders.
454.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Products without novel DNA combinations exempt from GMO regulation.

458.name: Malaysia
458.legislation: Biosafety Act 2007. Biosafety (Approval and Notifications) Regulations 2010
458.regulatory_body: National Biosafety Board (NBB), Department of Biosafety (DOB), Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources
458.summary: Malaysia's current regulatory framework under the Biosafety Act 2007 does not distinguish between GMOs and gene-edited crops, creating regulatory uncertainty for gene-editing research. Scientists have called for Malaysia to follow countries like Japan by exempting gene-edited crops without foreign DNA from GMO regulation. Active gene-editing research is underway, including work on gene-edited rice, but commercialisation prospects remain uncertain. During COP-MOP 11 in 2024, Malaysia supported balanced approaches on the classification of gene-edited organisms.
458.approach: Currently regulated under GMO framework. No specific gene-editing guidelines or exemptions.

470.name: Malta
470.legislation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 of the European Parliament and of the Council on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products
470.regulatory_body: European Commission and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)
470.summary: EU Parliament has voted to adopt new rules granting use of gene edited plants that are climate and pest resistant to support food security. The new EU rules split regulation of EU cultivate or imported products into one of two "New Genomic Techniques" (NGT) groups: NGT-1 (conventional-like) and NGT-2 (GMO-like). The EU Commission has prepared an implementation strategy of Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products to ensure the EU NGT framework becomes fully functional on 17 July 2028.
470.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. National authorities must verify that NGT plants belong to category 1 (NGT-1), but their offspring do not need to be subsequently verified.

480.name: Mauritius
480.summary: Mauritius is examining the status of genome editing within its existing legislation as of 2024. At least one genome editing project is underway in the country. Specific regulatory guidelines for gene-edited crops have not yet been published.

484.name: Mexico
484.legislation: Biosafety Act of Genetically Modified Organisms (2005)
484.regulatory_body: SEMARNAT (Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources), SENASICA (National Service of Agri-food Health, Safety, and Quality)
484.summary: Mexico has been deliberating on how to regulate gene editing separately from traditional GMOs since at least 2016, but no specific gene-editing framework has been enacted. Scientists across Mexico have called on the government to establish evidence-based regulations distinguishing CRISPR and similar technologies from GMOs. A 2021 presidential decree called for the phase-out of glyphosate and restrictions on GE corn importation, adding further complexity. SEMARNAT handles environmental risk assessment while SENASICA oversees agricultural health and safety.
484.approach: Currently no specific gene-editing framework. Gene-edited crops assessed under existing GMO biosafety legislation.

498.name: Moldova
498.summary: Moldova classifies genome-edited plants under the same regulatory framework as GMOs. Gene-edited plants may be imported but are prohibited from cultivation.
498.approach: Prohibitive for cultivation. Import permitted under GMO regulatory framework.

508.name: Mozambique
508.summary: Mozambique is examining the status of genome editing within its existing legislation as of 2024. At least three genome editing research projects are underway, and genetically modified crop field trials (including cassava) are taking place. Specific regulatory guidelines for gene-edited crops have not yet been published.

528.name: Netherlands
528.legislation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 of the European Parliament and of the Council on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products
528.regulatory_body: European Commission and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)
528.summary: EU Parliament has voted to adopt new rules granting use of gene edited plants that are climate and pest resistant to support food security. The new EU rules split regulation of EU cultivate or imported products into one of two "New Genomic Techniques" (NGT) groups: NGT-1 (conventional-like) and NGT-2 (GMO-like). The EU Commission has prepared an implementation strategy of Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products to ensure the EU NGT framework becomes fully functional on 17 July 2028.
528.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. National authorities must verify that NGT plants belong to category 1 (NGT-1), but their offspring do not need to be subsequently verified.

554.name: New Zealand
554.legislation: Hazardous Substances and New Organisms (HSNO) Act 1996. Gene Technology Bill 2024 (pending)
554.summary: New Zealand currently regulates gene-edited crops as GMOs under the HSNO Act 1996, one of the world's most stringent gene technology regulatory frameworks. A Gene Technology Bill was introduced to Parliament in December 2024, proposing a dedicated Gene Technology Regulator with a risk-tiered approval system separate from the HSNO framework. The bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Health Select Committee, which released a revised draft in October 2025. Cross-party disagreement has slowed progress, and the bill has not yet been enacted as of mid-2026.
554.approach: Precautionary. All genetic modifications currently assessed under HSNO framework. Reform legislation pending.

558.name: Nicaragua
558.legislation: Law 705, Prevention of Risks Arising from Organisms Derived from New Technologies through Molecular Biotechnology (2010)
558.regulatory_body: Institute of Agricultural Protection and Health (IPSA), Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (MARENA)
558.summary: Nicaragua's regulatory framework for biotechnology is governed by Law 705 (2010), though the law remains largely non-operational due to the absence of implementing regulations. The government advisory body CONARGEM was formed in 2004 to advise on GE crops. Nicaragua is a signatory to the Cartagena Protocol and requires notification for imports of GE crops. Under the current framework, engineered plants may be imported but not cultivated. No specific gene-editing exemption framework exists.
558.approach: Precautionary. GE crops may be imported but not cultivated. No distinction between GM and gene-edited products.

566.name: Nigeria
566.legislation: National Biosafety Management Agency (NBMA). National Biosafety Guidelines on Gene Editing, 2020
566.summary: Nigeria became the first African country to issue gene-editing guidelines when the NBMA authorised them in December 2020, with formal distribution in February 2022. The guidelines state that if a gene-edited product contains foreign DNA, it is classified as a GMO and is regulated under the NBMA 2015 Act & 2019 Amendment Act. In contrast, gene-edited products without foreign DNA will be subject to case-by-case regulatory provisions and may not need to undergo the full biosafety assessment process.

578.name: Norway
578.regulatory_body: Norwegian Scientific Committee for Food and Environment, Norwegian Environment Agency
578.summary: Norway updated its Gene Technology Act last year to maintain case-by-case testing of all GM and GEd products, while also aligning with the EU's future direction. However, if the EU redefines GMOs to exclude products of new genomic techniques (NGTs) from GM requirements, Norway must align due to its membership in the European Economic Area (EEA).

591.name: Panama
591.summary: Panama established a regulatory framework for gene-edited crops through Resolución CNB 008-2026, published in Gaceta Oficial No. 30559-D on 2 July 2026. The resolution creates a scientific assessment procedure allowing developers to request an official determination on whether their product qualifies as a GMO under Panamanian law. The classification criterion is whether the final organism contains a 'new combination of genetic material' as defined under the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety; products without novel genetic combinations may fall outside existing GMO legislation.
591.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Classification determined by presence or absence of a 'new combination of genetic material' per the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety.

600.name: Paraguay
600.legislation: Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock. Resolution No. 842/2019
600.regulatory_body: National Commission on Agricultural and Forestry Biosafety (CONBIO)
600.summary: Paraguay established its gene editing regulatory framework in 2019 through CONBIO Resolution No. 842. Classification is determined on a case-by-case basis according to whether the final product contains foreign DNA. Paraguay was among the earlier Latin American adopters of a GE-specific regulatory pathway, following Argentina, Brazil, and Chile.
600.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Classification determined by presence or absence of foreign DNA in the final product.

604.name: Peru
604.legislation: Ministry of Environment. Ministerial Resolution No. D000068-2026-MINAM-DM
604.summary: Peru's situation is distinctive due to the coexistence of a new GE classification framework with an active GMO moratorium. Law 29811 (2011), extended by Law 31111 to 31 December 2035, maintains a moratorium on Living Modified Organisms. Within this, MINAM approved Ministerial Resolution No. D000068-2026-MINAM-DM on 8 March 2026, establishing criteria to determine whether NBT-derived products fall within the scope of the moratorium. Transgene-free gene-edited products that do not meet the LMO definition may be classified as conventional.
604.approach: Definitional exclusion operating within an active GMO moratorium. Transgene-free products may be classified as conventional under criteria established March 2026.

608.name: Philippines
608.legislation: Executive Order No. 514 (2006), establishing National Biosafety Framework. Joint Department Circular No. 1 (JDC1) for Plant Breeding Innovations
608.regulatory_body: Department of Science and Technology (DOST), Department of Agriculture (DA), Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI)
608.summary: The Philippines regulates gene-edited crops through Joint Department Circular No. 1, signed by five departments (DOST, DA, DENR, DOH, DILG), which provides a technical evaluation process to classify whether products of plant breeding innovations (PBIs) are GMOs. Products without novel combinations of genetic material are issued a certificate of non-coverage. In April 2023, the BPI determined a gene-edited reduced-browning banana to be non-GE, the first product through this process. Additional gene-edited banana varieties were approved in June 2024.
608.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Technical evaluation determines whether products are classified as GMOs based on presence of novel genetic material.

616.name: Poland
616.legislation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 of the European Parliament and of the Council on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products
616.regulatory_body: European Commission and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)
616.summary: EU Parliament has voted to adopt new rules granting use of gene edited plants that are climate and pest resistant to support food security. 646.name: Rwanda
646.summary: Rwanda adopted gene-editing legislation in 2024, joining the growing number of African countries with biosafety frameworks. At least four genome editing research projects are underway. Rwanda is a party to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety and has developed a functional biosafety system.

702.name: Singapore
702.legislation: Singapore Food Agency. Regulatory Framework for the Use of Genome Edited Crops in Food and/or Animal Feed (August 2024)
702.summary: The SFA implemented a science-based, risk-proportionate regulatory framework for genome-edited crops on 1 August 2024. Genome-edited crops without foreign DNA that are equivalent to conventionally bred crops are not required to undergo pre-market safety assessment and are subject to the same monitoring as conventional crops. Genome-edited crops with foreign DNA are treated as GM crops and require full safety assessment. Developers of transgene-free genome-edited crops are encouraged to notify SFA through an Information Checklist.
702.approach: Product-based. Transgene-free genome-edited crops treated as conventional; those with foreign DNA treated as GM.

703.name: Slovakia
703.legislation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 of the European Parliament and of the Council on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products
703.regulatory_body: European Commission and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)

710.name: South Africa
710.legislation: Genetically Modified Organisms Act, 1997 (Act No. 15 of 1997)
710.regulatory_body: Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development
710.summary: South Africa regulates genome-edited crops as GMOs. In 2021, the government classified genome-edited plants as genetically modified under its interpretation of the GMO Act 1997. The Minister of Agriculture upheld this decision under section 19 of the Act, confirming that the risk assessment framework for GMOs also applies to new breeding techniques including gene editing. This approach places South Africa in contrast with several other African nations that have adopted science-based guidelines distinguishing gene editing from traditional GM.
710.approach: Process-based. All new breeding techniques including genome editing regulated under the GMO Act framework.

410.name: South Korea
410.regulatory_body: Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS), Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs (MAFRA)
410.summary: South Korea currently regulates gene-edited crops under the same framework as GMOs, requiring 'GMO' labelling even for gene-edited crops without foreign genes. The National Assembly passed the 'GMO Full Disclosure Act' (Food Sanitation Act Amendment). Scientists and industry have called for regulatory reform to distinguish gene editing from traditional GMOs, noting that Korea has technological competitiveness but lags in commercialisation speed. As of 2025, regulatory reform discussions are ongoing but no specific gene-editing exemption framework has been enacted.
410.approach: Currently regulated as GMO. Reform discussions ongoing.

724.name: Spain
724.legislation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 of the European Parliament and of the Council on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products
724.regulatory_body: European Commission and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)

752.name: Sweden
752.legislation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 of the European Parliament and of the Council on plants obtained by certain new genomic techniques and their products
752.regulatory_body: European Commission and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)
752.summary: EU Parliament has voted to adopt new rules granting use of gene edited plants that are climate and pest resistant to support food security. The new EU rules split regulation of EU cultivate or imported products into one of two "New Genomic Techniques" (NGT) groups: NGT-1 (conventional-like) and NGT-2 (GMO-like). 756.name: Switzerland
756.legislation: Gene Technology Act. Cultivation moratorium extended to 2030. Draft Breeding Technologies Act (consultation opened April 2025)
756.regulatory_body: Federal Council, Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)
756.summary: Switzerland maintains a cultivation moratorium on GMOs, extended through the end of 2030 in June 2025. The Federal Council opened consultation on a draft Breeding Technologies Act on 2 April 2025, proposing a risk-based authorisation procedure for plants from new breeding technologies. The proposal would exempt targeted mutagenesis (including CRISPR) from the strict GMO ban provided no transgenic DNA from unrelated species is present. Uniquely, the Swiss proposal requires modifications to respect the constitutional principle of 'Dignity of Living Beings'. The proposal faces significant opposition from environmental and consumer groups.
756.approach: Currently under moratorium. Proposed risk-based authorisation for plants from new breeding technologies.

764.name: Thailand
764.legislation: Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperatives. Certification of Organisms Developed from Genome Editing Technology for Agricultural Use, B.E. 2567 (2024)
764.regulatory_body: Department of Agriculture (DOA), Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperatives
764.summary: In July 2024, Thailand's Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperatives enacted the Certification of Organisms Developed from Genome Editing Technology for Agricultural Use, B.E. 2567. The Department of Agriculture published detailed notification criteria in the Royal Gazette on 15 August 2024. The regulation facilitates the safe development and commercial use of genome-edited plants, animals, and microorganisms in agriculture, with a certification process expected to take 2-3 months. The regulation aligns with Thailand's 'Ignite Agriculture Hub' initiative.
764.approach: Certification-based. Developers submit applications for certification of genome-edited organisms to the DOA.

800.name: Uganda
800.legislation: UNCST Standard Operating Procedures and guidelines. Biosafety Act 2017 & Genetic Engineering Regulatory Act (GERA) declined by the President 2019
800.regulatory_body: Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST), National Biosafety Committee (NBC)
800.summary: Uganda's biosafety regulation is managed by UNCST through Standard Operating Procedures and guidelines, as dedicated biosafety legislation remains absent. The President declined to assent to the Genetic Engineering Regulatory Act (GERA) in 2019 (drafting restarted 2022), creating uncertainty around GM and gene-editing regulation. UNCST through the NBC has been drafting guidelines for gene-edited crops, expected to exempt products without transgenes from the full GMO assessment. Active gene-editing research includes advanced banana trials.
800.approach: Guided by UNCST Standard Operating Procedures. Specific gene-editing guidelines under development.

858.name: Uruguay
858.legislation: Ministry of Livestock, Agriculture, and Fisheries / Ministry of Environment. Decree 84/024
858.regulatory_body: Ministry of Livestock, Agriculture, and Fisheries (MGAP)
858.summary: Uruguay established its gene editing regulatory framework through Decree 84/024, announced 18 March 2024, making it one of the more recent Latin American adopters. The decree established a Technical Working Group process to determine on a case-by-case basis whether a gene-edited product should be classified as a GMO, with the central criterion being the presence or absence of foreign DNA in the final product. Uruguay's framework is consistent with the broader regional convergence around the product-based foreign-DNA criterion that has emerged across Latin America since Argentina's 2015 decision.
858.approach: Product-based, case-by-case via Technical Working Group. Central criterion is presence or absence of foreign DNA.

840.name: United States
840.legislation: USDA APHIS Revised Biotechnology Regulations (SECURE Rule), 7 CFR Part 340 (2020, vacated December 2024). EPA, FDA co-regulate under Coordinated Framework for Regulation of Biotechnology
840.regulatory_body: USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
840.summary: The SECURE Rule, finalised in May 2020, shifted USDA from process-based to product-based regulation, exempting gene-edited plants that could have been developed through conventional breeding from regulation under 7 CFR Part 340. However, in December 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California vacated the SECURE Rule, and APHIS reinstated legacy pre-2020 regulations. The US regulatory framework operates through a Coordinated Framework involving USDA, EPA, and FDA. Despite the legal setback, gene-edited crops without foreign DNA have generally been treated as exempt from regulation across multiple administrations.
840.approach: Product-based. APHIS evaluates whether modified organisms pose increased plant pest risk compared to conventionally bred plants. Multi-agency oversight through the Coordinated Framework.

704.name: Vietnam
704.legislation: Government of Vietnam. Decree 43/2026/ND-CP (January 2026), implementing Law 146/2025/QH15 (Amended Law on Biodiversity)
704.summary: Vietnam formalised its distinction between GMOs and gene-edited crops through Decree 43/2026/ND-CP, issued 26 January 2026, implementing the amended Law on Biodiversity (Law 146/2025/QH15). Gene-edited organisms without foreign DNA are excluded from GMO regulatory requirements and eligible for a self-declaration process. The decree accelerates approval timelines for GE food and feed products from 90 to 45 working days for products already cleared in at least five OECD or G20 nations. The reform was driven by Party Resolution 57 (December 2024), which identified biotechnology as a strategic technology.
704.approach: Product-based. Gene-edited organisms without foreign DNA exempt from GMO requirements via self-declaration process.

894.name: Zambia
894.legislation: Biotechnology and Biosafety Policy (2003, under review)
894.summary: Zambia’s National Biotechnology and Biosafety Policy was enacted in 2003, followed by the Biosafety Act in 2007. In 2025, the National Biosafety Authority issued guidelines establishing the regulatory pathway for genome-edited plants. If foreign DNA remains in the final product, it is regulated as a GMO under the Biosafety Act. Products are not regulated under the Act when the edits: (a) involve inserts from sexually compatible species, (b) yield processed products in which foreign DNA is no longer detectable, (c) produce outcomes comparable to natural or conventionally bred variation, or (d) reach a stage at which the foreign DNA has been removed or segregated.

GB-ENG.name: England
GB-ENG.regulatory_body: Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA)
GB-ENG.summary: Post-Brexit, the UK diverged through a two-step reform, first easing field-trial requirements for gene-edited plants in 2022, followed by the Genetic Technology (Precision Breeding) Act 2023, which applies in England. The Act establishes a new category of Precision Bred Organisms (PBOs) for genetic changes that could have occurred naturally, enabling a streamlined route to market outside GMO regulations. In 2025, the Genetic Technology (Precision Breeding) Regulations 2025 were passed and came into force in November 2025, fully operationalising the framework for precision-bred plants.
GB-ENG.approach: Product-based, case-by-case. Marketing applications for Precision Bred Organisms (PBOs) can be put forward and are dealt by DEFRA and the Food Standards Agency (FSA)

GB-SCT.name: Scotland
GB-SCT.legislation: Scottish Government, Agriculture and Rural Economy Directorate
GB-SCT.regulatory_body: Science and Advice for Scottish Agriculture (SASA)
GB-SCT.summary: Unlike England, Scotland blocked the application of the Precision Breeding Bill. The Scottish goverment indicates that they will follow EU decisions on such legislation changes.
GB-SCT.approach: Precautionary, case-by-case approach where the scale of release is related to the level of risk. a GMO or a food product dervied from a GMO can only be put on the market in Scotland after it has been authorised on the basis of a detailed procedure based on a scientific assessment of the risks to health and the environment

GB-WLS.name: Wales
GB-WLS.legislation: Senedd Cymrus. Legislation, Justice and Constitution Committee
GB-WLS.regulatory_body: Food Standards Agency (FSA) and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)
GB-WLS.summary: Unlike England, Wales decided to not apply the Precision Breeding Act. This is due to concern that the UK government did not work with the Welsh government until the Bill's first reading, therefore lacking consideration on the Bill's impacts on Wales, among other reasons. Instead, Wales still consider gene editing as a form of genetic modification, in line with the European Court of Justice ruling in 2018.
GB-WLS.approach: Case-by-case, product-based approach. Formal authorization needs to be acquired at the EU level to ensure that foods do not present a risk to health

GB-NIR.name: Northern Ireland
GB-NIR.legislation: the Department of Agriculture and Rural development (DARD), Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (DAERA)
GB-NIR.regulatory_body: Health and Safety Executive for Northern Ireland (HSENI) and the Department of the Environment
GB-NIR.summary: Nothern Ireland did not enact England's Precision Breeding Bill. The country considers gene editing as a form of genetic modification, in line with the European Court of Justice ruling in 2018.
GB-NIR.approach: case-by-case, product-based. Formal authorization needs to be acquired at the EU level to ensure that foods do not present a risk to health
